summary: The note explains how the United States federal estate tax generally does not apply to assets left to a spouse or a federally recognized charity. It lists the per-person exemption amounts for estates of decedents dying in 2014 through 2016, notes that only the largest 0.2% of estates are estimated to pay the tax, and states that the exemption rises to $5.5 million in 2017 and doubles to $11.18 million in 2018 under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017.
one_line: Overview of US federal estate tax exemptions from 2014 to 2018, including spousal and charitable exclusions and the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act change.
key_facts: Assets left to a spouse or a federally recognized charity usually are not subject to the federal estate tax.
The federal gift and estate tax exemption was $5,340,000 for estates of persons dying in 2014 and 2015.
The federal gift and estate tax exemption was $5,450,000 for estates of persons dying in 2016.
The 2016 exemption equals effectively $10.90 million per married couple, assuming the deceased spouse did not leave assets to the surviving spouse.
It is estimated that only the largest 0.2% of estates in the U.S. will pay the estate tax, because of the exemptions.
For 2017, the estate tax exemption increases to $5.5 million.
In 2018, the exemption will double to $11.18 million per taxpayer.
The doubling of the exemption in 2018 is due to the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017.
The exemption is a maximum amount that an individual can give, before and/or upon death, without incurring federal gift or estate taxes.
The exemption amount varies year by year.

entities.name: Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017
entities.role: Legislation that doubles the estate tax exemption to $11.18 million per taxpayer in 2018
